items.prompt: What does TDD (test-driven development) mean, as this unit defines it?
choices: Writing a failing test for a small piece of behavior before writing the code that implements it
Writing tests after the feature is complete, to check for bugs
Running all existing tests before every commit
Writing extra documentation alongside every test file
items.explanation: The order is the defining feature — the test is written first, before the implementation exists, not afterward as a check.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: Two engineers each write a test and an implementation for the same feature. One writes the test first; one writes the implementation first, then a test. Which one is doing TDD?
choices: Only the one who wrote the test first
Both, since both end up with a test and an implementation
Neither, unless the tests use a specific testing framework
Only the one who wrote the implementation first, since that's more common
items.explanation: Having both a test and an implementation at the end doesn't make it TDD — the defining feature is the order, test before implementation.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: An engineer writes the full implementation of a feature, then writes a comprehensive test suite for it afterward, with 100% coverage. Is this TDD?
choices: No — regardless of how thorough the tests are, TDD specifically requires the test to be written before the implementation
Yes, since the end result includes both tests and implementation
Yes, as long as coverage is above 90%
It depends on which testing framework was used
items.explanation: Thoroughness after the fact doesn't substitute for the test-first order — TDD's design pressure specifically depends on the test existing before the implementation does.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: What are the three steps of the red-green-refactor loop, in order?
choices: Write a failing test, write minimum code to pass it, clean up the implementation
Write the implementation, write a test, delete unused code
Plan the feature, write all tests, write all code
Write code, run it manually, write documentation
items.explanation: Red (a failing test), green (minimum code to pass), refactor (clean up while staying green) — in that specific order, repeated for each small piece of behavior.
items.reference:
Red-green-refactor
red: write a failing test
green: minimum code to pass
refactor: clean up, stay green

Why: Each step has a specific job — skipping or reordering them loses what that step was guarding against.

items.prompt: In the red-green-refactor loop, what happens immediately after a test passes (green)?
choices: The refactor step — cleaning up the implementation while the passing test guards against breaking it
The loop ends permanently for that feature
All existing tests are deleted and rewritten
The next feature's tests are written before any refactoring happens
items.explanation: Refactor comes right after green, using the now-passing test as a safety net for cleaning up whatever shortcuts were taken to reach green quickly.
items.reference:
Red-green-refactor
red: write a failing test
green: minimum code to pass
refactor: clean up, stay green

Why: Each step has a specific job — skipping or reordering them loses what that step was guarding against.

items.prompt: Why does the test have to actually fail first (red), before any implementation is written?
choices: Watching it fail confirms the test is actually capable of failing, which is what makes it trustworthy when it later passes
It's a formality required by most testing frameworks
Failing tests run faster than passing ones
It has no real purpose beyond tradition
items.explanation: A test that passes the instant it's written might be trivially true rather than actually verifying anything — seeing it fail first rules that out.
items.reference:
Why red comes first
a test that can't fail proves nothing
seeing red first confirms it actually can

Why: Trusting a passing test later depends on having seen it capable of failing first.

items.prompt: What would it mean if a newly-written test passed immediately, with no implementation yet written for the behavior it's testing?
choices: The test may be trivially true or not actually exercising the intended behavior — it hasn't proven anything yet
It means the implementation was somehow already correct by coincidence
It means the test framework is broken
It's always a sign of excellent code quality
items.explanation: A test that passes with no implementation present is a warning sign, not a good outcome — it suggests the assertion isn't actually checking what it's supposed to.
items.reference:
Why red comes first
a test that can't fail proves nothing
seeing red first confirms it actually can

Why: Trusting a passing test later depends on having seen it capable of failing first.

items.prompt: What does 'minimum code to pass' mean in the green step?
choices: Writing only enough implementation to make the current failing test pass, nothing more
Writing code as short as possible in terms of character count
Skipping the implementation and only writing comments
Writing all anticipated future behavior at once, to save time later
items.explanation: The constraint is about scope, not brevity — implement exactly what the current test demands, deferring anything beyond that until a test actually requires it.
items.reference:
Minimum code to pass
only what the current test requires
extra code has no test proving it's needed

Why: Code written beyond the current test is an untested guess about future requirements.

items.prompt: Why is code written beyond what the current test requires considered risky?
choices: It has no test proving it's correct or even needed — it's a guess made without the pressure of a real assertion
It always runs slower than minimal code
Most compilers reject code that isn't covered by a test
It automatically introduces a security vulnerability
items.explanation: Untested code is a guess about a future requirement — nothing has verified it does what's actually needed, or that it's needed at all.
items.reference:
Minimum code to pass
only what the current test requires
extra code has no test proving it's needed

Why: Code written beyond the current test is an untested guess about future requirements.

items.prompt: What is 'design pressure,' as this unit uses the term?
choices: The effect of writing a test first: an interface that's hard to assert against gets noticed and reshaped immediately
The requirement that all code must pass a formal design review
A metric that measures how many design patterns a codebase uses
The pressure to finish a feature before a deadline
items.explanation: Design pressure is the immediate feedback test-first provides: if an assertion is awkward to write, that discomfort shows up before the interface even exists, not after.
items.reference:
Design pressure
hard-to-assert interface gets noticed early
before other code depends on it

Why: The pressure is about timing — the same problem exists either way, but test-first surfaces it before the interface is built.

items.prompt: Why does an awkward interface get noticed sooner under TDD than under a code-first approach?
choices: Because the assertion has to be written before the interface exists, so an awkward shape is uncomfortable immediately rather than discovered later
Because TDD requires a formal architecture review before any code is written
Because TDD only works with certain programming languages
Because code-first approaches never produce working software
items.explanation: Test-first forces the interface decision to happen at the moment the assertion is written — before any code exists to make that decision feel already settled.
items.reference:
Design pressure
hard-to-assert interface gets noticed early
before other code depends on it

Why: The pressure is about timing — the same problem exists either way, but test-first surfaces it before the interface is built.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why couldn't the code-first engineer's `console.warn`-based checker be easily reused in a UI?
choices: It has nothing an assertion — or a UI — could directly grab onto; the information only exists as printed text
console.warn is technically slower than returning a value
UIs are physically incapable of displaying any information originating from console.warn
The code-first version doesn't actually check passwords correctly
items.explanation: A UI needs structured data (like a score and a list of messages) to render — printed console text isn't something other code can consume directly.
items.reference:
Two starting points
console.warn: nothing to assert against
test-first: forced to return structured data

Why: The same design that's easiest to test tends to be the design that's easiest to reuse elsewhere.

items.prompt: Why did the test-first engineer end up with a function that returns `{ score, feedback }` instead of printing directly?
choices: Because writing `expect(...).toEqual(...)` before any implementation existed required something an assertion could compare against
Because returning objects is always faster than printing
Because the test-first engineer happened to personally prefer that style
Because console.warn doesn't exist in every programming language
items.explanation: The assertion itself demanded a comparable return value — that requirement existed before any implementation choice was made, not as a stylistic afterthought.
items.reference:
Two starting points
console.warn: nothing to assert against
test-first: forced to return structured data

Why: The same design that's easiest to test tends to be the design that's easiest to reuse elsewhere.

Slow test execution times

items.prompt: Does a single red-green-refactor cycle typically cover an entire feature at once?
choices: No — the loop repeats for each small piece of behavior, not the whole feature in one pass
Yes, one cycle should always implement the complete feature
Yes, but only for features with a single function
No, each cycle must cover exactly two behaviors at once
items.explanation: The loop is deliberately small-scoped — one cycle covers one small piece of behavior, with the whole feature emerging from several cycles in sequence.
items.reference:
Small steps
one cycle = one small piece of behavior
the full feature emerges from several cycles

Why: A cycle that tries to cover too much at once loses the tight feedback loop that makes red-green-refactor useful.

items.prompt: Why does the red-green-refactor loop deliberately stay scoped to small pieces of behavior, rather than tackling a whole feature per cycle?
choices: A smaller scope keeps each red-green-refactor cycle fast and gives a tight, specific feedback loop rather than a vague one
Because most programming languages impose a hard limit on function length
Because larger cycles are technically impossible to implement
Because small pieces of behavior never require any implementation code
items.explanation: Keeping each cycle small keeps the feedback specific and fast — a cycle covering too much behavior at once makes it harder to tell exactly what broke if the test fails.
items.reference:
Small steps
one cycle = one small piece of behavior
the full feature emerges from several cycles

Why: A cycle that tries to cover too much at once loses the tight feedback loop that makes red-green-refactor useful.

items.prompt: Is it acceptable for green-step code to be deliberately incomplete or incorrect for cases no test has covered yet?
choices: Yes — nothing yet requires that behavior to be correct, so a placeholder is fine until a test demands more
No, every possible input must be handled correctly starting from the very first green step
No, green-step code must always be production-ready immediately
Yes, but only if the placeholder is documented in a separate file
items.explanation: The minimum-code-to-pass constraint means it's expected, not sloppy, for green-step code to leave unaddressed cases as placeholders until a specific test requires handling them.
items.reference:
Deliberate placeholders
a case with no test yet can stay a placeholder
correctness is added only when a test demands it

Why: This is what "minimum code to pass" actually looks like in practice, not just in theory.

It's a bug that should have been caught immediately

It's acceptable only because the function is private

Deliberate placeholders

correctness is added only when a test demands it

items.prompt: Why is it safe to refactor aggressively once the green step's tests are passing?
choices: The existing tests keep passing throughout — any refactor that breaks behavior shows up immediately as a newly failing test
Refactoring is never actually risky, regardless of tests
Because refactoring automatically runs a full security audit
Because green-step code never contains any duplication to clean up
items.explanation: The tests already written act as a safety net — a refactor that accidentally changes behavior gets caught immediately, not discovered later as a bug.
items.reference:
Why refactor is safe
tests already exist and already pass

Why: Refactoring without tests is a leap of faith; refactoring with passing tests has an immediate correctness check.

items.prompt: Why is a separate refactor step needed instead of just moving on once a test passes?
choices: The green step's minimum-effort code often leaves duplication or awkward structure that's fine as a shortcut but not fine long-term
Because passing tests always contain bugs that must be fixed afterward
Because most testing frameworks require a refactor step by convention
Because refactoring is required to make the test suite run faster
items.explanation: Green optimizes for passing quickly, which can leave the implementation rougher than it needs to be — refactor is where that gets cleaned up deliberately.
items.reference:
Why refactor is safe
tests already exist and already pass
a behavior-breaking refactor fails a test immediately

Why: Refactoring without tests is a leap of faith; refactoring with passing tests has an immediate correctness check.

items.prompt: According to L2, what's the relationship between 'easiest to test' and 'easiest to reuse elsewhere'?
choices: They tend to be the same design — a pure function returning structured data satisfies both
They're always in direct conflict with each other
There's no meaningful relationship between the two
Easiest to reuse always means slower to test
items.explanation: A function that returns comparable, structured data is both easy to assert against and easy to plug into a UI, an API, or another check — the two properties converge.
items.reference:
Why the two properties converge
testable = returns comparable data
reusable = returns comparable data
same shape, two benefits

Why: Test-first doesn't forbid the untestable design — it just removes the delay before that design's cost becomes visible.

items.prompt: Does writing implementation first forbid ever landing on a testable, reusable design?

Yes, code-first approaches can never produce a testable design
Yes, but only for functions with more than one parameter
No, code-first and test-first always produce identical designs
items.explanation: Test-first isn't the only path to a good design — it just surfaces the awkwardness of a bad one immediately, rather than after other code has already been built around it.
items.reference:
Why the two properties converge
testable = returns comparable data
reusable = returns comparable data
same shape, two benefits

Why: Test-first doesn't forbid the untestable design — it just removes the delay before that design's cost becomes visible.

items.prompt: Does TDD guarantee good design?
choices: No — it's possible to write technically-passing tests against a bad interface and never notice, especially with loosely written tests
Yes, following red-green-refactor always produces a well-designed interface
Yes, but only for functions with fewer than three parameters
No, TDD makes design meaningfully worse in every case
items.explanation: TDD provides an early moment to notice an awkward interface, but whether that moment actually gets used to improve the design is still a separate judgment call.
items.reference:
What TDD actually guarantees
a specific early moment to confront the interface
not an automatic guarantee that moment gets used well

Why: A loosely written or tautological test can pass against a genuinely bad interface without anyone noticing.
